# INTRAVASCULAR CATHETER-ASSOCIATED GRAM-NEGATIVE BACILLI INFECTION

Catheter removal is strongly recommended, especially when resistant isolates are present. Delayed catheter removal is associated with increased mortality in patients with drug resistant organisms. The decision about whether to remove the catheter depends on severity of illness, presence of resistant organisms, the need for the catheter, and how difficult catheter replacement would be.

References:
Mandell chapter: Infections Caused by Percutaneous Intravascular Devices
Mermel et al., Clinical Infectious Diseases 49 (2009)
Up-to-Date article gram-negative bacillary bacteremia in adults
Up-to-date article: Intravascular catheter-related infection: Epidemiology, pathogenesis, and microbiology
Up-to-date article: Intravascular non-hemodialysis catheter-related infection: Treatment
Therapy:
## Inpatient/Outpatient

## Treatment if catheter is removed (preferred)

Duration of therapy:
Treat uncomplicated cases for 7 to 14 days. A longer duration may be required for complicated or critically ill patients. Consult Infectious Diseases for more information.

Refer to specific isolate bacteremia recommendations for selection of antimicrobial.
[Citrobacter Freundii, Klebsiella Aerogenes or Enterobacter Cloacae bacteremia](citrobacter-freundii-bacteremia)
[Pseudomonas sp. bacteremia](pseudomonas-bacteremia)
[Other Gram-negatives bacteremia](other-gram-negative-rods-bacteremia)

## Treatment if catheter removal is not possible (less desirable)

Duration of therapy:
Treat uncomplicated cases with concurrent systemic and antibiotic lock therapy for 14 days. A longer duration may be required for complicated or critically ill patients.

## Consult Infectious Diseases in all cases.

Treatment:
Add antimicrobial lock therapy to systemic treatment
<ADD> gentamicin antibiotic lock therapy
